clinicalPearls: A rare cause of bilateral, rapidly progressive sensorineural hearing loss evolving over weeks to months
The tempo is faster than age-related loss but slower than sudden sensorineural hearing loss
Vestibular symptoms such as imbalance and dizziness may accompany the hearing loss
It may be primary (isolated to the ear) or secondary to a systemic autoimmune disease such as vasculitis or Cogan syndrome
A response to a trial of corticosteroids supports the diagnosis, which lacks a specific confirmatory test
Prompt immunosuppressive treatment offers the best chance of preserving hearing
reference.pathophysiology: Autoimmune inner ear disease is thought to result from immune-mediated injury to cochlear and vestibular structures, whether through antibodies, immune complexes or cell-mediated mechanisms directed at inner ear antigens. The resulting inflammation damages the cochlea and sometimes the vestibular apparatus, producing progressive sensorineural hearing loss and imbalance. In secondary forms the inner ear is one target of a broader systemic autoimmune or vasculitic process, and the potential reversibility with early immunosuppression reflects the immune rather than purely degenerative basis.
additionalDifferentials: Vestibular schwannoma or other retrocochlear lesion
additionalInvestigations: Serial audiometry to document progression and treatment response
Assessment for systemic autoimmune disease and vasculitis
MRI to exclude a retrocochlear lesion
Investigations to exclude otosyphilis and other infective causes
Monitored trial of corticosteroids as a diagnostic and therapeutic step
redFlags: Features of systemic vasculitis or Cogan syndrome
Asymmetric loss suggesting a retrocochlear tumour
reference.prognosis: Hearing can be preserved or partially recovered if immunosuppression is started early, but delayed treatment often results in permanent loss; cochlear implantation may help advanced cases.
pitfalls: Attributing progressive bilateral loss to presbyacusis and missing a treatable cause
Failing to exclude otosyphilis and retrocochlear lesions
Delaying corticosteroids while awaiting non-specific tests
Overlooking an underlying systemic autoimmune disease
